title: Social Security (Administration) Amendment (Continuation of Cashless Welfare) Bill 2020
short_title: Social Security (Administration) Amendment (Continuation of Cashless Welfare) Bill 2020

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: The bill would make the Cashless Debit Card an ongoing program instead of a trial.
It would also bring people in the Northern Territory and Cape York who are on Income Management onto the Cashless Debit Card and let people in Bundaberg and Hervey Bay volunteer for the program.
The bill would extend the program's sunset date to 31 December 2021.
changes: Removes trial parameters to make the Cashless Debit Card a permanent program.
Transitions Income Management participants in the Northern Territory and Cape York to the Cashless Debit Card.
Lets people in Bundaberg and Hervey Bay volunteer for the program.
Allows voluntary participants to stay in the program even if they leave a program area.
Enables the Secretary to issue and revoke participant notices.
summary.affected: People receiving welfare payments in certain areas, including those in the Northern Territory, Cape York, Bundaberg and Hervey Bay, and voluntary participants.

The usual second reading motion is "*that the bill be [read a second time](https://peo.gov.au/understand-our-parliament/how-parliament-works/bills-and-laws/making-a-law-in-the-australian-parliament/)*," which is parliamentary jargon for agreeing with the main idea of the bill. This division took place after the MP for Barton [Linda Burney](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/representatives/barton/linda_burney) (Labor) proposed an amendment to the usual second reading motion. ### Amendment text > *That all words after "That" be omitted with a view to substituting the following words:* > > *"the House declines to give the bill a second reading and:* > > *(1) notes that:* > >> *(a) thirteen years after the Howard Government's so-called Intervention in the Northern Territory, there is no evidence that compulsory, broad-based income management works;* >> >> *(b) the Minister decided to make the Cashless Debit Card trial permanent before reading the independent review by Adelaide University; and* >> >> *(c) this proposal is racially discriminatory, as approximately 68 per cent of the people impacted are First Nations Australians; and* > > *(2) calls on the Government to:* > >> *(a) not roll out the Cashless Debit Card nationally; and* >> >> *(b) invest in evidence-based policies, job creation and services, rather than ideological policies like the Cashless Debit Card"* ### What does the bill do? The majority voted in favour of a [motion](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?id=2020-12-08.15.2): > *that the [Social Security (Administration) Amendment (Continuation of Cashless Welfare) Bill 2020](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query%3DId%3A%22legislation%2Fbillhome%2Fr6608%22) be included with the other bills exempt from the cut-off order.* In other words, they wanted to suspend the usual procedural rules - known as [standing orders](https://peo.gov.au/understand-our-parliament/how-parliament-works/parliament-at-work/standing-orders/) - so that they can consider the Social Security (Administration) Amendment (Continuation of Cashless Welfare) Bill 2020 during this sitting period.

The majority voted in favour of a [motion](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2020-12-09.158.1) introduced by South Australian Senator [Simon Birmingham](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/senate/sa/simon_birmingham) (Liberal), which means it passed. ### Motion text > *That today:* > > *(a) the hours of meeting be 9.30 am to adjournment;* > > *(b) if, by 7.20 pm, the [Social Security (Administration) Amendment (Continuation of Cashless Welfare) Bill 2020](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query%3DId%3A%22legislation%2Fbillhome%2Fr6608%22) has not been finally considered, the routine of business from that time be consideration of the bill only;* > > *(c) if, by midnight, consideration of the bill has not been completed, the questions on all remaining stages be put without debate;* > > *(d) paragraph (c) operate as a limitation of debate under standing order 142;* > > *(e) divisions may take place after 7.20 pm for the purposes of the bill only; and* > > *(f) the Senate adjourn without debate after the consideration of the bill, or when the adjournment is proposed by a minister, whichever is earlier.*

The majority voted against a [motion](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2020-12-09.199.1) moved by WA Senator [Rachel Siewert](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/senate/wa/rachel_siewert) (Greens), which means it failed. ### Motion text > *At the end of the motion, add ", but the Senate:* > > *(a) notes that:* > >> *(i) this bill will entrench the racist, discriminatory, paternalistic, ineffective, top-down, blanket approach of compulsory income management via the Cashless Debit Card,* >> >> *(ii) the Government did not consult with First Nations peoples in the Northern Territory about the introduction of the Cashless Debit Card or the continuation of compulsory income management, and* >> >> *(iii) the Government failed to consult with people currently on the Cashless Debit Card about making it permanent; and* > > *(b) calls on the Government to:* > >> *(i) abandon all forms of compulsory income management currently operating in Australia,* >> >> *(ii) carry out extensive consultation around Australia for any move to make income management voluntary and ensure that any new program is co-designed, and* >> >> *(iii) immediately release the second impact evaluation being undertaken by the University of Adelaide".* ### What does this bill do? The [bill was introduced](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd2021a/21bd033) "*to establish the [Cashless Debit Card](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cashless_Welfare_Card) (CDC) as an ongoing program rather than a time-limited trial*". The CDC program is controversial for many reasons, not least the [limited evidence](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2020-11-16/little-data-cashless-debit-card-effective-unisa-researcher-says/12887258) that it is benefiting the communities where it is currently in operation. Read more about the program and what the bill does in the [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd2021a/21bd033).

The majority voted in favour of an [amendment](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2020-12-09.201.1) to the usual second reading motion, which is "*that the bill be read a [second time](https://www.peo.gov.au/understand-our-parliament/how-parliament-works/bills-and-laws/making-a-law-in-the-australian-parliament/)*" (parliamentary jargon for agreeing with the main idea of the bill). It was introduced by SA Senator [Rex Patrick](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/senate/sa/rex_patrick) (Independent). Note that, while this amendment was successful, it doesn't make any changes to the bill itself. ### Amendment text > *At the end of the motion, add ", but the Senate calls on the Government to provide a commitment that no recipient of the Age Pension or a Veteran or Service Pension will be placed on the Cashless Debit Card, with the exception of those who volunteer or are referred by the Family Responsibility Commission, child protection workers, social workers or the Alcohol Mandatory Treatment Tribunal in the Northern Territory".* ### What does this bill do? speeches.speaker: Linda Burney
speeches.brief: The speaker opposed the Social Security (Administration) Amendment (Continuation of Cashless Welfare) Bill 2020, arguing it is racially discriminatory—68% of those affected are First Nations Australians—and lacks evidence, as the minister decided to make the Cashless Debit Card permanent before reading the independent Adelaide University evaluation. The speaker moved an amendment to decline the bill and called for investing in evidence-based policies, job creation and services instead of the card.

speeches.speaker: Rick Wilson
speeches.brief: The speaker argued for the continuation of the cashless debit card trial in the Goldfields, citing positive impacts such as reduced alcohol-related harm, improved child welfare, and community support, with 276 exit applications (87 approved) and 151 wellbeing applications (106 granted). They criticised senators for not visiting trial sites and thanked local leaders including Gay Harris, Patrick Hill, and Betty Logan for their advocacy.

speeches.speaker: Warren Snowdon
speeches.brief: The speaker opposed the Social Security (Administration) Amendment (Continuation of Cashless Welfare) Bill 2020, arguing it disregards Aboriginal communities and noting 68% of those impacted are First Nations people. They highlighted that the minister had not read the $2.5 million review before introducing the bill and cited Aboriginal Peak Organisations Northern Territory’s statements that compulsory income management has a "disabling" effect and denies basic freedoms.

speeches.speaker: Rowan Ramsey
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the original motion for the Social Security (Administration) Amendment (Continuation of Cashless Welfare) Bill 2020 but opposed the amendment, arguing the cashless welfare card has been successful in Ceduna with broad community support and should be made permanent rather than renewed annually. He rejected claims of racial discrimination or expansion to age pensioners, and noted that increased unrestricted cash during COVID led to more antisocial behaviour in Ceduna.

speeches.speaker: Kate Thwaites
speeches.brief: The speaker opposed the Social Security (Administration) Amendment (Continuation of Cashless Welfare) Bill 2020, arguing it is based on ideology rather than evidence and discriminates against First Nations people. The speaker cited research showing negative impacts, including stigma, insufficient cash for essentials, and that 68% of those affected (over 23,000 of 34,000 people) are Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander, and criticised the government for proceeding without reading a relevant review.

speeches.speaker: Tony Pasin
speeches.brief: The speaker argued for the continuation of the Cashless Welfare Bill, citing personal experience as a criminal lawyer seeing children harmed by parental alcohol, drug and gambling abuse, and rejected claims of racial discrimination, stating the program applies geographically. He supported restricting 80% of welfare payments to essentials, claiming it leads to better outcomes for vulnerable children.

speeches.speaker: Rebekha Sharkie
speeches.brief: The speaker argued against making the cashless welfare card permanent and expanding it to new locations, citing the government's failure to release the University of Adelaide evaluation report and the lack of promised rehabilitation services and education opportunities in trial sites like Ceduna. Centre Alliance will not support the bill but would back a continued trial extension if the government provides rehabilitation facilities, education courses, and proper consultation, particularly for remote Indigenous communities.

speeches.speaker: Julian Simmonds
speeches.brief: The speaker argued for the Social Security (Administration) Amendment (Continuation of Cashless Welfare) Bill 2020, citing evidence of reduced alcohol and gambling harm and citing ANU evaluation findings. Concrete figures mentioned include youth unemployment in Bundaberg and Hervey Bay dropping from 28% in May 2018 to 18.1% in May 2019.

speeches.speaker: Adam Bandt
speeches.brief: The Greens opposed the bill to make cashless welfare card trials permanent and extend them to over 25,000 people in the Northern Territory, arguing it disempowers Indigenous Australians, lacks evidence, and violates the National Agreement on Closing the Gap.

speeches.speaker: Jason Falinski
speeches.brief: The speaker argued for making the cashless debit card trials permanent in Ceduna, East Kimberley, Bundaberg, Hervey Bay, the Northern Territory and Cape York, affecting 25,000 people on income management and 12,500 already using the card, stating the bill saves lives and improves opportunities for disadvantaged Australians.

speeches.speaker: Joanne Ryan
speeches.brief: The speaker opposed the cashless debit card, arguing it has shifted from a community‑agreed trial to a draconian measure that causes shame and stigma, and noted her own experience as a single mother on welfare.

speeches.speaker: Ged Kearney
speeches.brief: The speaker opposed the Cashless Welfare Bill, arguing it lacks evidence, was made permanent before an independent review, and is racially discriminatory—with around 68% of those affected being First Nations Australians. They called for the bill to be halted and for investment in evidence‑based policies, job creation, and services instead.

speeches.speaker: Graham Perrett
speeches.brief: Labor opposed the bill, arguing it makes permanent cashless debit card trial sites without local community support or evidence of effectiveness, and that 68% of those forced onto the card are First Nations Australians.

speeches.speaker: Elizabeth Coker
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Social Security (Administration) Amendment (Continuation of Cashless Welfare) Bill is discriminatory and racist, disproportionately affecting First Nations people, and that the minister responsible did not read the independent University of Adelaide review before proceeding. The speaker announced Labor's opposition to the bill, calling for it to be rejected.

speeches.speaker: Sharon Claydon
speeches.brief: The speaker opposed the Social Security (Administration) Amendment (Continuation of Cashless Welfare) Bill 2020, arguing it permanently imposes a racist, punitive cashless debit card system in Ceduna, the East Kimberley, the Goldfields, Bundaberg and Hervey Bay, and the entire Northern Territory, while failing to address underlying poverty or provide an exit strategy from income management.

speeches.speaker: Luke Gosling
speeches.brief: The speaker opposed the bill to permanently replace the BasicsCard with the cashless debit card in the Northern Territory, arguing it is racially discriminatory, lacks evidence of reducing harm, and was rushed without proper consultation—including the minister not reading a $2.5 million review. The card would affect over 23,000 people in the NT, two-thirds of whom are Indigenous, and communities overwhelmingly do not want it.

speeches.speaker: Lisa Chesters
speeches.brief: The speaker opposed the Social Security (Administration) Amendment (Continuation of Cashless Welfare) Bill 2020, arguing that the compulsory cashless debit card is a blunt instrument with no substantiated evidence of effectiveness, disproportionately targets First Nations communities, and that voluntary cards are preferable.

speeches.speaker: Mike Freelander
speeches.brief: The speaker opposed the Social Security (Administration) Amendment (Continuation of Cashless Welfare) Bill 2020, arguing it is discriminatory, lacks evidence, and would permanently place 35,000 people—70% of them First Nations—on the cashless debit card, despite opposition from communities, the Auditor-General, and an independent review still underway.

speeches.speaker: Peta Murphy
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the cashless welfare card is racist, stigmatises recipients, and disproportionately affects First Nations people, contrasting it with voluntary credit card use. They demanded the minister rule out extending the card to other welfare recipients, questioned the evidence base for the policy, and accused the Prime Minister of contradicting his February commitment to Indigenous self-determination.

speeches.speaker: Stephen Jones
speeches.brief: The speaker opposed the Social Security (Administration) Amendment (Continuation of Cashless Welfare) Bill 2020, arguing it divides Australians into two classes, ignores Indigenous voices and expert evidence (including ANU and University of Adelaide studies showing no reduction in domestic violence), and relies on outdated stereotypes of the unemployed—noting that 20% of Australians aged 55–65 are unemployed.
